headline: High: shared mounted-volume and MCP surfaces create default write/conflict and prompt-injection pathways; compliance risk is lower but nonzero.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: agent_a uses MCP and stdin/stdout, while agent_b exposes MCP servers and browser/file surfaces. That creates a plausible instruction-smuggling path if one agent’s output is routed into the other’s tool context or shared files. The pair lacks documented provenance controls, so uncertainty pushes above low.
conditions: IF agent_a output is copied into agent_b prompts or files without provenance tags
IF either agent parses MCP/file content as instructions
mitigations: Disable automatic ingestion of peer outputs
Add provenance markers to all inter-agent messages
Restrict MCP servers to read-only for both agents
Review any file-to-prompt bridge before enabling
requires-engineering: add content-sanitization and instruction-separation guards

B_data_leakage.rationale: agent_b reads and writes files in a mounted runtime, and agent_a can use MCP plus GitHub/network egress. If they share a workspace or mounted volume, agent_a’s touched code, repository metadata, and task prompts can flow into agent_b’s runtime and then out through its broader network surface. The shared-volume path is documented only indirectly, so medium is the safer choice.
conditions: IF both agents are attached to the same mounted volume or workspace
IF agent_b is given files containing agent_a prompts, code, or repository metadata
mitigations: Separate workspaces per agent
Mount only the minimum required directories
Remove secrets from shared files before handoff
Turn off network egress for any agent handling sensitive files
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent storage isolation

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can execute shell commands, install packages, modify git state, spawn subprocesses, and use MCP. agent_b explicitly supports shared state via mounted volume, so concurrent writes to the same repo or runtime can race and corrupt git or filesystem state. Because defaults include overlapping write capabilities, this is a high-risk conflict.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout or mounted directory
IF both agents run concurrently without external locking
mitigations: Run only one writer per repository at a time
Use separate clones or volumes
Pause one agent before the other mutates git state
Add a lockfile around shared mutable resources
requires-engineering: implement orchestrator-level concurrency locks

D_cascading_error.rationale: agent_a can generate analysis and repository changes, and agent_b has an agent loop with shell/browser/editor actions that can act on upstream output. If agent_b treats agent_a’s output as authoritative without verification, errors can cascade into edits or actions. The pair does not document a built-in verification barrier, so medium is warranted.
conditions: IF agent_b consumes agent_a output as task instructions or facts
IF no human or automated verification step is inserted between them
mitigations: Require a review step before execution
Ask agent_b to restate assumptions before acting
Limit agent_b to drafting, not committing, on first pass
Compare outputs against source files before use
requires-engineering: add structured validation between agents

E_compliance.rationale: agent_a handles task prompts and repository metadata, while agent_b handles files in a runtime and model-provider API keys. The profiles do not show a clear residency or certification mismatch, so only a low compliance concern is visible from docs. The risk is narrower than B because no specific regulated data class is documented.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into the shared runtime or prompts
IF the runtime or model provider is subject to a stricter retention policy than the repository workflow
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared prompts
Confirm retention settings for the model provider
Document which files may enter the runtime
Delete temporary artifacts after each run
requires-engineering: align residency and retention policies
